questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: NCERT notes that the classical definition of a hormone (a chemical produced by an endocrine gland, released into the blood and carried to a distantly located target organ) has only limited current scope. Hormones are now defined as non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts. Why is the newer definition preferred?

options.text: It restricts the term hormone to the secretions of the organised endocrine glands only
It includes nutrients such as glucose and amino acids that cells need in large amounts
It covers a number of new molecules in addition to the hormones secreted by the organised endocrine glands
It applies only to invertebrates, which have very simple endocrine systems

solution.explanation: NCERT: the new definition covers a number of new molecules in addition to the hormones secreted by the organised endocrine glands. The old definition tied a hormone to an organised gland and to transport in the blood to a distant organ, which leaves out many chemical messengers known today.
steps: Old definition: organised gland -> blood -> distant target
New definition: any non-nutrient intercellular messenger made in trace amounts
So it also covers new molecules not made by organised glands
solution.why_others_wrong: The newer definition widens, not narrows, the term; it explicitly says non-nutrient and trace amounts, so nutrients needed in bulk are excluded; and it applies to vertebrates too, which have many hormones.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Endocrine Glands and Hormones
solution.final_answer: Option C: It covers a number of new molecules in addition to the hormones secreted by the organised endocrine glands

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, under-production of hormones by the adrenal cortex causes acute weakness and fatigue, leading to Addison's disease. This happens because the under-production alters:

options.text: The calcium balance between bones and blood
Pigmentation, by acting on the melanocytes

solution.explanation: NCERT: underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue, leading to a disease called Addison's disease. (Glucocorticoids such as cortisol are the corticoids involved in carbohydrate metabolism.)
steps: Adrenal cortex hormones (glucocorticoids) regulate carbohydrate metabolism
Too little of them -> carbohydrate metabolism altered -> weakness and fatigue
solution.why_others_wrong: Calcium balance is the work of PTH and TCT, the diurnal rhythm is regulated by melatonin of the pineal, and pigmentation by MSH; none of these is how NCERT explains Addison's disease.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Adrenal Gland
solution.final_answer: Option A: Carbohydrate metabolism

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The follicular cells of the thyroid gland synthesise two hormones. One of them, thyroxine (T₄), is chemically:

solution.explanation: NCERT: the follicular cells synthesise two hormones, tetraiodothyronine or thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃). The subscript gives the number of iodine atoms, which is why iodine is essential for their normal rate of synthesis.
solution.why_others_wrong: Triiodothyronine is T₃, the other follicular hormone; thyrocalcitonin is a protein hormone of the thyroid that regulates blood calcium; TSH is made by the anterior pituitary, not the thyroid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Thyroid Gland
solution.final_answer: Option D: Tetraiodothyronine

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, what does the formation of a hormone-receptor complex in a target tissue lead to?

options.text: Destruction of the target cell, so that the hormone is released back into the blood
Certain biochemical changes in the target tissue, through which its metabolism and physiological functions are regulated
Secretion of the same hormone by the target cell, which then acts back on the endocrine gland
Conversion of the hormone into a nutrient that the target cell uses as a source of energy

solution.explanation: NCERT: hormone-receptor complex formation leads to certain biochemical changes in the target tissue. Target tissue metabolism, and hence physiological functions, are regulated by hormones in this way.
steps: Hormone binds its specific receptor -> hormone-receptor complex
Complex -> biochemical changes in the target tissue -> metabolism and functions regulated
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT says nothing of cell destruction or of the target cell secreting the same hormone, and hormones are defined as non-nutrient chemicals, so they are not used as an energy source.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Mechanism of Hormone Action
solution.final_answer: Option B: Certain biochemical changes in the target tissue, through which its metabolism and physiological functions are regulated

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Iodine is essential for the normal rate of hormone synthesis in the thyroid gland.
Statement II: Parathyroid hormone, along with thyrocalcitonin, plays a significant role in calcium balance in the body.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Statement I is NCERT's own line on iodine and thyroid hormone synthesis. Statement II is also NCERT: PTH is hypercalcemic and, along with TCT (a protein hormone of the thyroid that regulates blood calcium levels), plays a significant role in calcium balance.
steps: Statement I: true (iodine needed for T₄/T₃ synthesis)
Statement II: true (PTH + TCT -> calcium balance)
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct NCERT statements, so every option that calls either of them false is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Thyroid Gland; Parathyroid Gland
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
How many of the following hormones are secreted by the pars distalis of the human pituitary?

Growth hormone, MSH, prolactin, vasopressin, ACTH, oxytocin, FSH, TSH

solution.explanation: NCERT: the pars distalis produces GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH. The pars intermedia secretes only one hormone, MSH. Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesised by the hypothalamus and released from the neurohypophysis (pars nervosa). From the list, GH, prolactin, ACTH, FSH and TSH are pars distalis hormones.
steps: Pars distalis: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH
In the list: GH, prolactin, ACTH, FSH, TSH = 5
MSH -> pars intermedia; vasopressin, oxytocin -> released from the neurohypophysis
solution.why_others_wrong: Six counts MSH (pars intermedia) or one of the neurohypophysis hormones; eight counts every hormone; four leaves out one of GH, prolactin, ACTH, FSH or TSH.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', The Pituitary Gland
solution.final_answer: Option B: Five

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following disorders result from too little of a hormone (hyposecretion or impaired release) rather than from too much of it?

(a) Cretinism
(b) Acromegaly
(c) Pituitary dwarfism
(d) Exophthalmic goitre
(e) Diabetes insipidus

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: cretinism results from hypothyroidism during pregnancy; pituitary dwarfism from low secretion of growth hormone; diabetes insipidus from impaired synthesis or release of ADH. Acromegaly is due to excess growth hormone in adults, and exophthalmic goitre is a form of hyperthyroidism.
solution.why_others_wrong: Every wrong option includes acromegaly (excess GH) or exophthalmic goitre (excess thyroid hormone), which are disorders of over-secretion.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', The Pituitary Gland; Thyroid Gland
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (hormone) with List-II (cells or tissue on which NCERT says it mainly acts).

List-I:
A. Glucagon
B. Insulin
C. Aldosterone
D. MSH

List-II:
I. Melanocytes
II. Renal tubules
III. Hepatocytes and adipocytes
IV. Hepatocytes (liver cells)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: glucagon acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes); insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes (cells of adipose tissue); aldosterone acts mainly at the renal tubules; MSH acts on the melanocytes and regulates pigmentation of the skin.
solution.why_others_wrong: The trap is glucagon versus insulin: glucagon acts mainly on hepatocytes alone, insulin on hepatocytes and adipocytes. The other wrong codes swap aldosterone (kidney) with MSH (melanocytes) or with glucagon.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', The Pituitary Gland; Adrenal Gland; Pancreas
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A hormone released into the blood reaches almost all the tissues of the body, yet it acts only on certain tissues.
Reason (R): Hormones produce their effects by binding to specific hormone receptors, which are located in the target tissues only.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: hormones produce their effects on target tissues by binding to specific proteins called hormone receptors located in the target tissues only. So although the blood carries a hormone everywhere, only the tissues that have its receptors respond. R is the reason for A.
steps: A: true - the blood carries the hormone widely but only target tissues respond
R: true - receptors are present in target tissues only
No receptor -> no hormone-receptor complex -> no effect, so R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and the location of receptors only in target tissues is exactly why other tissues do not respond, so the options saying R is not the explanation, or that either is false, are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Mechanism of Hormone Action
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (secretion of the adrenal gland) with List-II (action described in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Cortisol
B. Aldosterone
C. Adrenaline
D. Androgenic steroids of the adrenal cortex

List-II:
I. Growth of axial hair, pubic hair and facial hair during puberty
II. Increased heartbeat, pupillary dilation and piloerection in an emergency
III. Reabsorption of Na⁺ and water, and excretion of K⁺ and phosphate ions, by the renal tubules
IV. Anti-inflammatory reactions and suppression of the immune response

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Hormones of the adrenal cortex and medulla
solution.explanation: NCERT: cortisol produces anti-inflammatory reactions and suppresses the immune response; aldosterone acts at the renal tubules, stimulating reabsorption of Na⁺ and water and excretion of K⁺ and phosphate ions; adrenaline (a catecholamine of the medulla) increases heartbeat, alertness, pupillary dilation, piloerection and sweating; small amounts of androgenic steroids from the cortex play a role in the growth of axial, pubic and facial hair during puberty.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the two corticoids (glucocorticoid action versus mineralocorticoid action), give adrenaline the hair-growth role of the adrenal androgens, or give aldosterone the emergency actions of the medulla.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Adrenal Gland
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the human body, androgens are secreted only by the Leydig cells of the testis.
Statement II: Androgens act on the central neural system and influence male sexual behaviour (libido).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Statement I is false: besides the Leydig cells, NCERT says the adrenal cortex also secretes small amounts of androgenic steroids, which play a role in the growth of axial, pubic and facial hair during puberty. Statement II is NCERT's description of androgen action.
steps: Statement I: false - the adrenal cortex also secretes small amounts of androgenic steroids
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I fails because of the word 'only'; Statement II is correct, so 'both true', 'both false' and 'I true, II false' are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Adrenal Gland; Testis
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: In a woman with otherwise normal hormone levels, the anterior pituitary fails to produce the rapid mid-cycle surge of LH, although FSH secretion and the growth of the follicles are normal. Which outcome is expected in that cycle?

options.text: Ovulation occurs normally, but the endometrium fails to regenerate during the follicular phase
The Graafian follicle does not rupture, so no ovum is released and no corpus luteum forms to secrete progesterone
The corpus luteum forms but secretes mainly estrogen instead of progesterone
Follicles fail to grow beyond the primary stage because estrogen is not secreted

solution.concept: Role of LH in ovulation and the corpus luteum
solution.explanation: NCERT: in females, LH induces ovulation of fully mature (Graafian) follicles and maintains the corpus luteum formed from the remnants of the Graafian follicle after ovulation. The rapid secretion of LH in mid-cycle (LH surge) induces rupture of the Graafian follicle. Without the surge the follicle does not rupture, so no ovum is released, no corpus luteum forms, and the progesterone it would secrete is not produced.
steps: Follicles grow (FSH normal) up to the Graafian stage
No LH surge -> Graafian follicle does not rupture -> no ovulation
No ovulation -> no corpus luteum -> no luteal progesterone
solution.why_others_wrong: Ovulation itself needs the LH surge, so it cannot occur normally; no corpus luteum can form without ovulation; and the stem says FSH and follicle growth are normal, so follicles do develop and secrete estrogen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', The Pituitary Gland; also Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Menstrual Cycle
solution.final_answer: Option B: The Graafian follicle does not rupture, so no ovum is released and no corpus luteum forms to secrete progesterone

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A person's β-cells secrete normal amounts of insulin, but the hepatocytes and adipocytes lack functional insulin receptors. Which of the following is expected?

options.text: Blood glucose falls sharply, because unbound insulin acts directly on the genome of the target cells
Blood glucose stays normal, because glucagon receptors take over the action of insulin
Blood glucose stays normal, because insulin enters the cells and acts without any receptor
Blood glucose stays high, because insulin can act on its target cells only after binding to its specific receptors

solution.concept: Hormones act only through their receptors
solution.explanation: NCERT: hormones produce their effects only by binding to specific receptors in the target tissues, and each receptor is specific to one hormone. Insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes to enhance cellular glucose uptake and utilisation. If these cells have no working insulin receptors, insulin in the blood cannot form a hormone-receptor complex, glucose is not moved from the blood into these cells, and blood glucose stays high even though insulin is present.
steps: No receptor on target cells -> no hormone-receptor complex -> no effect
Glucose uptake by hepatocytes and adipocytes not enhanced -> hyperglycemia persists
solution.why_others_wrong: Unbound hormone has no effect; receptors are specific, so glucagon receptors cannot respond to insulin (and glucagon raises blood sugar anyway); and NCERT says hormones act through receptors, not without them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Mechanism of Hormone Action; Pancreas
solution.final_answer: Option D: Blood glucose stays high, because insulin can act on its target cells only after binding to its specific receptors

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A tumour of the adrenal cortex secretes excess cortisol. Based on the actions of glucocorticoids described in NCERT, which of the following are expected?

(a) Increased gluconeogenesis, tending to raise the blood glucose level
(b) Suppression of the immune response
(c) Increased cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids
(d) Increased production of RBCs
(e) Increased secretion of adrenaline by the adrenal cortex

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis and inhibit cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids; cortisol produces anti-inflammatory reactions and suppresses the immune response; cortisol stimulates RBC production. Adrenaline is a hormone of the adrenal medulla, not the cortex.
steps: (c) false - amino acid uptake is inhibited
(e) false - adrenaline comes from the medulla
solution.why_others_wrong: (c) reverses the NCERT action (glucocorticoids inhibit amino-acid uptake and utilisation), and (e) gives the cortex a medullary hormone, so any option containing them is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Adrenal Gland
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre) is seen in iodine deficiency, a hypothyroid condition.
Statement II: Enlargement of the thyroid gland is also seen in exophthalmic goitre, a condition in which the basal metabolic rate is increased.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: deficiency of iodine in the diet results in hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly called goitre. Exophthalmic goitre is a form of hyperthyroidism characterised by enlargement of the thyroid gland, protrusion of the eyeballs, increased basal metabolic rate and weight loss. So an enlarged thyroid by itself does not tell whether thyroid hormone is too little or too much.
steps: Statement I: true - iodine deficiency -> hypothyroidism + goitre
Statement II: true - exophthalmic goitre (hyperthyroid) also has an enlarged thyroid, with raised BMR
solution.why_others_wrong: Students often link an enlarged thyroid only with iodine deficiency and mark Statement II false, but NCERT describes thyroid enlargement in both conditions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', Thyroid Gland
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a man whose pituitary secretes FSH normally but no LH, the secretion of androgens remains normal.
Reason (R): In males, LH acts on the Leydig cells and stimulates the synthesis and secretion of androgens.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: R is NCERT's description of LH action in males. Because LH is the hormone that stimulates the Leydig cells, a man with no LH would have low androgen secretion even if FSH is normal; FSH (with androgens) regulates spermatogenesis but does not drive androgen synthesis. So A is false.
steps: R: true - LH stimulates Leydig cells to make androgens
No LH -> Leydig cells not stimulated -> androgens fall
Normal FSH does not replace LH, so A is false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so the two 'both true' options and 'A true but R false' are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, Ch 19 'Chemical Coordination and Integration', The Pituitary Gland; Testis
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Each human testis has about 250 compartments called testicular lobules, and each lobule contains one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules. On this basis, the number of seminiferous tubules in one testis is expected to lie in the range of about:

solution.explanation: NCERT: each testis has about 250 testicular lobules, and each lobule contains one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules. Minimum = 250 x 1 = 250; maximum = 250 x 3 = 750.
solution.why_others_wrong: 83 to 250 divides instead of multiplying; 250 to 500 takes at most two tubules per lobule; 500 to 1,500 counts both testes, not one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Male Reproductive System
solution.final_answer: Option B: 250 to 750

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, parturition (the delivery of the foetus at the end of pregnancy) is induced by:

options.text: A purely neural reflex of the mother, without the involvement of any hormone
A sudden fall in hCG secreted by the corpus luteum
Uterine contractions caused by estrogens from the growing ovarian follicles

solution.explanation: NCERT: parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism. Signals from the fully developed foetus and the placenta induce mild uterine contractions (foetal ejection reflex), which trigger the release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary.
steps: Foetal and placental signals -> foetal ejection reflex -> oxytocin -> stronger contractions
solution.why_others_wrong: Oxytocin, a hormone, is part of the mechanism, so it is not purely neural; hCG is made by the placenta, not the corpus luteum; growing follicles and their estrogens are not part of NCERT's account of parturition.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Pregnancy and Embryonic Development; Parturition and Lactation
solution.final_answer: Option C: A complex neuroendocrine mechanism

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The seminiferous tubules of the human testis open into the vasa efferentia through the:

solution.explanation: NCERT: the seminiferous tubules of the testis open into the vasa efferentia through the rete testis. The vasa efferentia leave the testis and open into the epididymis.
steps: Seminiferous tubules -> rete testis -> vasa efferentia -> epididymis
solution.why_others_wrong: The epididymis lies after the vasa efferentia, the ejaculatory duct is formed where the vas deferens receives the duct of the seminal vesicle, and the urethral meatus is the external opening of the urethra.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Male Reproductive System
solution.final_answer: Option D: Rete testis

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Counting each gland separately, how many male accessory glands are present in a human male?

solution.explanation: NCERT: the male accessory glands include paired seminal vesicles, a prostate and paired bulbourethral glands. Counting each gland separately: 2 + 1 + 2 = 5.
solution.why_others_wrong: Three counts only the kinds of gland; four treats one pair as single; six wrongly makes the prostate paired.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Male Reproductive System
solution.final_answer: Option C: Five

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The testes of a human male are situated outside the abdominal cavity, within a pouch called the scrotum.
Reason (R): Each testis has about 250 compartments called testicular lobules.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Position and structure of the testis
solution.explanation: Both are NCERT facts. A is about where the testes lie (the scrotum keeps them 2-2.5 °C below body temperature, which is needed for spermatogenesis). R is about the internal structure of the testis. The number of lobules has nothing to do with the position of the testes, so R does not explain A.
steps: R describes internal structure, not the reason for the position -> not the explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so the options calling either false are wrong; the reason for the scrotal position is temperature, not the number of lobules, so R is not the correct explanation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Male Reproductive System
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Spermatogonia present on the inside wall of the seminiferous tubules multiply by mitotic division and increase in number.
Statement II: Primary spermatocytes contain 23 chromosomes each.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: spermatogonia, the diploid male germ cells on the inside wall of the seminiferous tubules, multiply by mitosis. Some of them, called primary spermatocytes, periodically undergo meiosis. A primary spermatocyte has not yet divided by meiosis, so it is diploid with 46 chromosomes; only after the first meiotic division do the secondary spermatocytes have 23 chromosomes.
steps: Statement II: false - primary spermatocytes have 46; secondary spermatocytes have 23
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses primary with secondary spermatocytes, so the options calling it true are wrong; Statement I is correct, so 'both false' and 'I false, II true' are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Gametogenesis
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: In a human female, 25 primary oocytes complete the first meiotic division. Every secondary oocyte so formed is then entered by a sperm and completes the second meiotic division. Assuming that the first polar bodies do not divide further, how many polar bodies are formed in all?

solution.explanation: NCERT: the primary oocyte completes the first meiotic division, an unequal division forming a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. When a sperm enters, the secondary oocyte completes the second meiotic division, again unequal, forming a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid). Each primary oocyte therefore gives 1 ovum and, here, 2 polar bodies: 25 x 2 = 50.
steps: Per primary oocyte: 1 first polar body + 1 second polar body = 2
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 counts only one polar body per oocyte; 75 adds the ova to the polar bodies; 100 assumes four products per oocyte as in spermatogenesis.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Gametogenesis
solution.final_answer: Option B: 50

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which of the following shows the correct path of milk in the human mammary gland, from the cells that secrete it to the duct through which it is sucked out?

options.text: Alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct
Alveoli → mammary duct → mammary tubules → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct
Alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary ampulla → mammary duct → lactiferous duct
Mammary tubules → alveoli → mammary duct → lactiferous duct → mammary ampulla

solution.explanation: NCERT: the cells of the alveoli secrete milk, stored in the cavities of the alveoli. The alveoli open into mammary tubules. The tubules of each lobe join to form a mammary duct. Several mammary ducts join to form a wider mammary ampulla, which is connected to the lactiferous duct through which milk is sucked out.
steps: Tubules of a lobe -> mammary duct
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong sequence swaps two neighbouring parts: tubules and duct, duct and ampulla, or starts from the tubules instead of the milk-secreting alveoli.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Female Reproductive System
solution.final_answer: Option A: Alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The human zygote divides by mitosis (cleavage), forming 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells called blastomeres. NCERT calls an embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres a morula. Assuming every blastomere divides at each round, after which numbers of completed rounds of cleavage is the embryo in this range?

solution.explanation: Number of blastomeres after n rounds = 2ⁿ. 2³ = 8 and 2⁴ = 16, so the embryo has 8 to 16 blastomeres after 3 and after 4 rounds of cleavage. After 2 rounds it has only 4 cells; after 5 rounds it would have 32.
solution.why_others_wrong: Two rounds give only 4 cells and five rounds give 32; '8 and 16 rounds' confuses the number of cells with the number of divisions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Fertilisation and Implantation
solution.final_answer: Option C: After 3 and after 4 rounds

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Each spermatid formed in a human male contains 46 chromosomes.
Reason (R): Spermatids are formed when the secondary spermatocytes undergo the second meiotic division.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: R is NCERT's description: the secondary spermatocytes undergo the second meiotic division to produce four equal, haploid spermatids. The secondary spermatocytes already have only 23 chromosomes after the first meiotic division, so each spermatid has 23 chromosomes, not 46. A is false.
steps: Primary spermatocyte (46) -> meiosis I -> secondary spermatocytes (23 each)
Meiosis II -> spermatids (23 each), so A is false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false because spermatids are haploid, so the options that call A true are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Gametogenesis
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (cell) with List-II (where it is found).

List-I:
A. Sertoli cells
B. Leydig cells
C. Granulosa cells
D. Theca

List-II:
I. In the interstitial spaces outside the seminiferous tubules
II. Around the oocyte in an ovarian follicle, starting as a single layer in the primary follicle
III. Inside the seminiferous tubules, where they provide nutrition to the germ cells
IV. Around the secondary follicle, organised into an inner and an outer layer in the tertiary follicle

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Somatic cells of the testis and of ovarian follicles
solution.explanation: NCERT: each seminiferous tubule is lined by spermatogonia and Sertoli cells, which provide nutrition to the germ cells; the Leydig (interstitial) cells lie in the interstitial spaces outside the tubules. A primary oocyte surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells is a primary follicle; a secondary follicle has more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca; in the tertiary follicle the theca is organised into an inner theca interna and an outer theca externa.
solution.why_others_wrong: Sertoli cells are inside the tubules and Leydig cells outside, so swapping them is wrong; the granulosa layer is present from the primary follicle, whereas the theca appears only in the secondary follicle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Male Reproductive System; Gametogenesis
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (process) with List-II (kind of cell division involved).

List-I:
A. Cleavage of the zygote
B. Formation of spermatids from secondary spermatocytes
C. Spermiogenesis
D. Formation of the secondary oocyte from the primary oocyte

List-II:
I. First meiotic division, unequal
II. Mitosis
III. Second meiotic division
IV. No cell division (transformation of a cell)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: cleavage is the mitotic division of the zygote; secondary spermatocytes undergo the second meiotic division to form spermatids; spermiogenesis transforms spermatids into spermatozoa without any division; the primary oocyte completes the first meiotic division, an unequal division, forming the secondary oocyte and the first polar body.
solution.why_others_wrong: Spermatids come from the second, not the first, meiotic division; cleavage is a true division (mitosis), whereas spermiogenesis involves no division; and the primary oocyte must divide (meiosis I) to give the secondary oocyte.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Gametogenesis; Fertilisation and Implantation
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following events of oogenesis take place in a human female before her birth, that is, during her fetal life?

(a) Formation of a couple of million gamete mother cells (oogonia) within each fetal ovary
(b) Entry of these cells into prophase-I of meiosis, where they are temporarily arrested as primary oocytes
(c) Completion of the first meiotic division to form the secondary oocyte
(d) Formation of a fluid-filled cavity called the antrum in the follicle
(e) Completion of the second meiotic division to form the ovum

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: oogenesis is initiated during embryonic development, when a couple of million oogonia are formed within each fetal ovary; no more are formed after birth. These cells enter prophase-I of meiosis and are temporarily arrested as primary oocytes. The first meiotic division is completed within the tertiary follicle (after puberty, as follicles mature); the antrum appears in the tertiary follicle; the second meiotic division is completed only when a sperm enters the secondary oocyte.
steps: (c) in the tertiary follicle, after puberty
solution.why_others_wrong: Meiosis I is completed only in the tertiary follicle, the antrum belongs to the tertiary follicle, and meiosis II is completed at fertilisation, so (c), (d) and (e) are not fetal events.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Gametogenesis
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a) and (b) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium because its trophoblast cells divide rapidly and cover it.
Statement II: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst gets differentiated as the embryo.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the trophoblast layer gets attached to the endometrium and the inner cell mass gets differentiated as the embryo. After attachment, it is the uterine cells that divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst, so that it becomes embedded in the endometrium (implantation). Statement I gives the dividing cells wrongly.
steps: Statement I: false - the uterine cells, not the trophoblast, divide and cover the blastocyst
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false and Statement II true; the other three combinations do not fit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Fertilisation and Implantation
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Normally only one sperm fertilises a human ovum.
Reason (R): Contact of a sperm with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum induces changes in the membrane that block the entry of additional sperms.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Prevention of entry of more than one sperm
solution.explanation: NCERT: during fertilisation a sperm comes in contact with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum and induces changes in the membrane that block the entry of additional sperms. Thus it ensures that only one sperm can fertilise an ovum. R gives the mechanism of A.
steps: The membrane change after the first sperm's contact blocks other sperms -> R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and NCERT itself links them ('thus it ensures that only one sperm can fertilise an ovum'), so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Fertilisation and Implantation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If a woman's corpus luteum kept secreting large amounts of progesterone beyond the end of her usual cycle, her endometrium would be maintained and menstruation would be delayed.
Statement II: In the absence of fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, and this causes disintegration of the endometrium.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in the luteal phase the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, which is essential for maintenance of the endometrium; in the absence of fertilisation the corpus luteum degenerates, causing disintegration of the endometrium and leading to menstruation. It follows that continued progesterone secretion would keep the endometrium and delay menstruation - as indeed happens in pregnancy, when there is no menstruation.
steps: Statement I: progesterone maintains the endometrium; its fall (corpus luteum degeneration) causes menstruation -> sustained progesterone delays menstruation -> true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I follows directly from the role of progesterone in maintaining the endometrium, and Statement II is NCERT text, so no option calling either false is correct.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Menstrual Cycle
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
In a man, both seminal vesicles and the prostate are absent from birth, but the testes, the duct system and the bulbourethral glands are normal. Which of the following are expected?

(a) Sperms are still formed in the seminiferous tubules.
(b) The volume of seminal plasma in his ejaculate is reduced.
(c) The maturation and motility of his sperms may be affected.
(d) Androgen secretion by his Leydig cells stops.
(e) Secretions of the bulbourethral glands are still available for lubrication of the penis.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Roles of the male accessory glands
solution.explanation: NCERT: the secretions of the male accessory glands (seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands) constitute the seminal plasma; the secretions of the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate are essential for maturation and motility of sperms; bulbourethral secretions help in lubrication of the penis. Sperm formation and androgen secretion take place in the testis, which is normal.
steps: (b) two of the three kinds of accessory gland missing -> less seminal plasma
(c) seminal vesicle and prostate secretions are essential for maturation and motility
(d) false - Leydig cells are in the normal testis
solution.why_others_wrong: (d) is wrong because androgens come from the Leydig cells of the testis, which is normal; the options that leave out (b) or (c) ignore NCERT's role of these glands in seminal plasma and in sperm maturation and motility.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Male Reproductive System
solution.final_answer: Option C: (a), (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (defect) with List-II (most likely consequence).

List-I:
A. The fimbriae of the infundibulum do not function
B. After the trophoblast attaches, the uterine cells fail to divide
C. The acrosome of the sperms lacks its enzymes
D. The lactiferous ducts of a lactating mother are blocked

List-II:
I. Milk secreted in the alveoli cannot be sucked out
II. The sperm cannot enter the ovum through the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane
III. The blastocyst is not covered and embedded, so implantation fails
IV. The ovum released at ovulation is not collected into the oviduct

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: the fimbriae help in collection of the ovum after ovulation; after the trophoblast attaches, the uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst, embedding it (implantation); secretions of the acrosome help the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the ovum through the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane; milk is sucked out through the lactiferous duct.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong code gives one defect the consequence of another: fimbriae act before fertilisation (collecting the ovum), the uterine cells act at implantation, the acrosome at sperm entry, and the lactiferous duct in milk removal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', The Female Reproductive System; Fertilisation and Implantation
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
During pregnancy the levels of several hormones rise in the mother's blood. Which of the following are hormones whose levels increase several-fold during pregnancy but which are ALSO produced in women who are not pregnant?

(a) Estrogens
(b) hCG
(c) Prolactin
(d) hPL (human placental lactogen)
(e) Progestogens

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: hCG and hPL are produced in women only during pregnancy (by the placenta). In addition, during pregnancy the levels of other hormones, including estrogens, progestogens and prolactin, are increased several-fold in the maternal blood; these hormones are also made in women who are not pregnant (estrogens and progesterone by the ovary, prolactin by the anterior pituitary).
steps: Only in pregnancy (placental): hCG, hPL -> (b), (d) excluded
Increased several-fold but made anyway: estrogens, prolactin, progestogens -> (a), (c), (e)
solution.why_others_wrong: hCG and hPL are the trap: they are placental hormones produced in women only during pregnancy, so any option containing (b) or (d) is wrong; '(b) and (d) only' answers the opposite question.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Pregnancy and Embryonic Development
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: In a human foetus, the heart has formed and its sound can be heard through a stethoscope, but the limbs and digits have not yet developed. According to the timeline given in NCERT, the pregnancy is most likely:

options.text: In the fifth month, when the first movements of the foetus are usually observed
Between about one and two months old
At about 24 weeks, at the end of the second trimester
At about 12 weeks, when most of the major organ systems have formed

solution.explanation: NCERT: after one month of pregnancy the embryo's heart is formed, and the first sign of the growing foetus may be noticed by listening to the heart sound through a stethoscope. By the end of the second month the foetus develops limbs and digits. So a foetus with a heart but no limbs and digits is between about one and two months old.
steps: Limbs and digits: by the end of the second month
Heart present, limbs absent -> between one and two months
solution.why_others_wrong: By 12 weeks, the fifth month and 24 weeks the limbs and digits (formed by the end of the second month) are already present, so none of these fits a foetus without limbs.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 2 'Human Reproduction', Pregnancy and Embryonic Development
solution.final_answer: Option B: Between about one and two months old

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A woman had unprotected coitus at 9 p.m. on a Monday. According to NCERT, emergency contraceptives (progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations, or IUDs) are very effective if used within 72 hours of coitus. By what time at the latest should she use one?

solution.explanation: NCERT: administration of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus has been found to be very effective as emergency contraceptives. 72 hours = 3 days, and 3 days after 9 p.m. on Monday is 9 p.m. on Thursday.
solution.why_others_wrong: Wednesday allows only 48 hours, Friday 96 hours and the following Monday a full week; only Thursday is 72 hours later.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option B: 9 p.m. on Thursday

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists only of copper-releasing intra-uterine devices (IUDs)?

solution.explanation: NCERT: IUDs are non-medicated (e.g., Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) or hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20).
solution.why_others_wrong: Lippes loop is non-medicated, and Progestasert and LNG-20 are hormone-releasing IUDs, so each of the other pairs contains at least one IUD that does not release copper.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option C: CuT and Multiload 375

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A young person had unprotected sex with an unknown partner a few weeks ago and has noticed no symptoms so far. According to NCERT, what is the best course of action?

options.text: Go to a qualified doctor for early detection, and get complete treatment if an infection is diagnosed
Wait until symptoms appear, since an STI without symptoms is harmless
Start taking oral contraceptive pills, which also protect against STIs
Avoid going to a doctor, since STIs cannot be detected until AIDS develops

solution.explanation: NCERT: early symptoms of STIs are minor, and infected persons (especially females) may often be asymptomatic, so infections may remain undetected for long. One of the simple principles for prevention is: in case of doubt, go to a qualified doctor for early detection and get complete treatment if diagnosed with an infection. Many STIs are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.
steps: STIs often show absent or less significant early symptoms
Doubt -> qualified doctor -> early detection -> complete treatment
solution.why_others_wrong: Untreated STIs can lead to PID, infertility and other complications even when symptoms are minor; oral pills give no protection against STIs; and STIs can be detected early, which is why NCERT stresses early detection.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Go to a qualified doctor for early detection, and get complete treatment if an infection is diagnosed

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Natural methods of contraception have almost no side effects.
Reason (R): No medicines or devices are used in natural methods of contraception.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: natural methods (periodic abstinence, withdrawal, lactational amenorrhea) work on the principle of avoiding the chances of the ovum and sperms meeting. As no medicines or devices are used in these methods, side effects are almost nil (though chances of failure are high). R is the stated reason for A.
steps: NCERT: 'as no medicines or devices are used ... side effects are almost nil' -> R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and NCERT gives R as the reason for A, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A woman who relies only on a hormone-releasing IUD is not protected against STIs from an infected partner.
Statement II: Because an IUD acts inside the uterus, it also destroys the viruses that cause hepatitis-B and HIV.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms; they are not barriers. Of the contraceptives, NCERT credits condoms with protecting the user from STIs and AIDS, because they prevent contact with semen. So an IUD user is not protected against STIs (Statement I true), and nothing in NCERT says IUDs destroy viruses (Statement II false).
steps: Statement I: true - IUDs do not stop the passage of infection during coitus
Statement II: false - IUDs act on sperms and implantation, not on viruses
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false, so 'both true' and 'I false, II true' are wrong; Statement I is true, so 'both false' is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods); Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
According to NCERT, which of the following are features of an ideal contraceptive?

(a) It should be user-friendly and easily available.
(b) It should be effective.
(c) It should be reversible, with no or the least side effects.
(d) It should in no way interfere with the sexual drive, desire and/or the sexual act of the user.
(e) It should permanently stop the formation of gametes.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: an ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible with no or least side-effects; it also should in no way interfere with the sexual drive, desire and/or the sexual act of the user. A method that permanently stops gamete formation would be irreversible.
solution.why_others_wrong: (e) contradicts reversibility, so any option containing it is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (situation) with List-II (assisted reproductive technology that suits it).

List-I:
A. A woman cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation in her oviduct
B. The male partner is unable to inseminate the female, or has very low sperm counts
C. An embryo with more than 8 blastomeres formed in vitro is to be transferred
D. A sperm is to be injected directly into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory

List-II:
I. Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)
II. Intra uterine transfer (IUT)
III. Artificial insemination (AI) or intra-uterine insemination (IUI)
IV. Gamete intra fallopian transfer (GIFT)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: GIFT is the transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation; AI (into the vagina or, as IUI, into the uterus) is used where the male cannot inseminate or has very low sperm counts; embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are transferred into the uterus (IUT); in ICSI a sperm is directly injected into the ovum.
solution.why_others_wrong: GIFT and IUT differ in what is transferred and where (an ovum into the oviduct versus an embryo into the uterus); AI places semen in the female tract, whereas ICSI injects a single sperm into an ovum in the laboratory.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Assisted Reproductive Technologies
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A mother is still breast-feeding her baby fully, eight months after parturition, and relies on lactational amenorrhea as her only method of contraception. According to NCERT, which statement applies to her?

options.text: The method remains effective for as long as she breast-feeds, however long that is
The method is considered effective only up to a maximum of six months after parturition, so she should not rely on it alone now
The method is effective only in the first two weeks after parturition
The method works by blocking the fallopian tubes, so its effect is permanent

solution.explanation: NCERT: lactational amenorrhea is based on the fact that ovulation, and therefore the cycle, do not occur during the period of intense lactation following parturition; it has been reported to be effective only up to a maximum period of six months following parturition. At eight months she is beyond that period.
steps: LAM effective up to a maximum of six months after parturition
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT puts the limit at six months, not 'as long as she breast-feeds' or two weeks; and lactational amenorrhea acts by the absence of ovulation during intense lactation, not by blocking the tubes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option B: The method is considered effective only up to a maximum of six months after parturition, so she should not rely on it alone now

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In GIFT, fertilisation takes place in the laboratory before the gametes are transferred into the fallopian tube.
Statement II: In ZIFT, the zygote or an early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in GIFT, an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation; fertilisation therefore takes place inside her body (in vivo). In ZIFT, the zygote or early embryos (with up to 8 blastomeres), formed in vitro, are transferred into the fallopian tube.
steps: Statement I: false - in GIFT a gamete is transferred and fertilisation happens in the oviduct
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I describes ZIFT, not GIFT; Statement II is correct, so only 'I false, II true' fits.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Assisted Reproductive Technologies
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Vasectomy stops the production of sperms in the testes.
Reason (R): In vasectomy, a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: R is NCERT's description of vasectomy. The operation is on the vas deferens, a duct that carries sperms from the epididymis towards the urethra; it blocks gamete transport and thereby prevents conception. The testes (seminiferous tubules) are untouched, so sperm production is not stopped. A is false.
steps: R: true - vas deferens cut or tied
Testes untouched -> sperm production continues -> A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so the two 'both true' options and 'A true but R false' are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A couple wants a child. Both fallopian tubes of the wife are completely blocked, but she produces normal ova and has a normal uterus. The husband has a very low sperm count. Which of the following techniques described in NCERT could help them?

(a) In vitro fertilisation followed by transfer of the embryo into her uterus (IUT)
(b) Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), followed by transfer of the embryo into her uterus
(c) Gamete intra fallopian transfer (GIFT)
(d) Zygote intra fallopian transfer (ZIFT)
(e) Intra-uterine insemination (IUI) alone

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Choosing ART when the oviducts are blocked
solution.explanation: With both oviducts blocked, any technique that places gametes or embryos in the fallopian tube (GIFT, ZIFT) cannot work, and IUI alone cannot work because the sperms still have to meet the ovum in the oviduct. Fertilisation must therefore be done in the laboratory and the embryo placed in the uterus: IVF with IUT, or ICSI (a sperm injected directly into the ovum, useful when sperms are few) with transfer into the uterus.
steps: Oviducts blocked -> no GIFT, no ZIFT, no IUI
Uterus normal -> embryo can be placed in the uterus
IVF + IUT and ICSI + transfer into the uterus both bypass the oviduct
solution.why_others_wrong: GIFT and ZIFT need a working fallopian tube, and IUI depends on fertilisation in the oviduct, so options containing (c), (d) or (e) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Assisted Reproductive Technologies
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a) and (b) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (method) with List-II (limitation stated in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Lactational amenorrhea
B. Emergency contraceptives
C. Surgical methods (sterilisation)
D. Periodic abstinence and coitus interruptus

List-II:
I. Chances of failure are high
II. Reversibility is very poor
III. Very effective only if used within 72 hours of coitus
IV. Effective only up to a maximum period of six months following parturition

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: lactational amenorrhea is effective only up to a maximum of six months after parturition; emergency contraceptives are very effective within 72 hours of coitus; reversibility of sterilisation is very poor; natural methods such as periodic abstinence and withdrawal have almost no side effects but their chances of failure are high.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the two time limits (six months versus 72 hours) or give sterilisation the high failure rate of natural methods; sterilisation is very effective but poorly reversible.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 3 'Reproductive Health', Birth Control (Contraceptive Methods)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of contraceptive methods prevent conception WITHOUT preventing ovulation?

solution.explanation: NCERT: condoms are barriers that prevent the meeting of ovum and sperms, and vasectomy blocks sperm transport; neither affects ovulation. questions.subject: Zoology

solution.concept: Hardy-Weinberg from a ratio of homozygotes
solution.explanation: p² = 4q², so p = 2q (frequencies are positive). With p + q = 1: 3q = 1, q = 1/3 and p = 2/3. Frequency of Aa = 2pq = 2 x 2/3 x 1/3 = 4/9.

A biologist follows a gene with two alleles in a population over several generations. Which of the following observations would indicate that the population is NOT in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

questions.question_text: A circular vector of 4.4 kb has a single BamHI site. A 1.6 kb DNA fragment with BamHI sticky ends at both ends is ligated into this site. 4.4 kb; a single fragment of 4.4 kb
6.0 kb; a single linear fragment of 6.0 kb

Circular DNA with n sites -> n fragments -> 4.4 kb and 1.6 kb

A palindrome in DNA reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same (5' → 3'). How many of the following double-stranded sequences, each given as its upper (5' → 3') strand, are palindromes?

5'-GTTAAC-3', 5'-CTGCAG-3', 5'-GATATC-3', 5'-AGCTAG-3', 5'-GAACTC-3'

solution.explanation: Write the complementary strand and read it 5' → 3' (that is, take the reverse complement). GTTAAC -> GTTAAC, CTGCAG -> CTGCAG and GATATC -> GATATC are palindromes. AGCTAG -> CTAGCT and GAACTC -> GAGTTC are not.
solution.shortcut: A DNA palindrome equals its own reverse complement.
solution.why_others_wrong: Reading the second strand in the same direction is the test; counting AGCTAG or GAACTC uses the plain complement or a simple reversal instead of the reverse complement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Three

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: EcoRI recognises 5'-GAATTC-3' (complementary strand 3'-CTTAAG-5') and cuts each strand between the bases G and A. What is the single-stranded overhang on each sticky end produced?

options.text: No overhang, since EcoRI gives blunt ends

solution.explanation: Cutting the upper strand G^AATTC and the lower strand (read 5' → 3', also G^AATTC) leaves each fragment with a single-stranded stretch of 5'-AATT-3'. Because the site is palindromic, both sticky ends carry the same overhang, which is why they can pair with each other by hydrogen bonds.
solution.why_others_wrong: GAAT would need a cut between T and C; a two-base overhang would need a cut in the middle of the other strand; and NCERT shows EcoRI producing sticky, not blunt, ends.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option A: 5'-AATT-3' on each end

Match List-I (step or component of PCR) with List-II (what happens or why it is used).

solution.explanation: NCERT: each PCR cycle has three steps: denaturation (high temperature separates the strands), annealing (the two sets of primers bind to complementary regions) and extension (DNA polymerase extends the primers using the nucleotides provided and the genomic DNA as template). A thermostable DNA polymerase, isolated from Thermus aquaticus, is used because it remains active during the high-temperature denaturation.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap denaturation with annealing, annealing with extension, or extension with the reason for using a thermostable enzyme.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Amplification of gene of interest using PCR)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
A restriction digest gives three DNA fragments of 0.5 kb, 2 kb and 5 kb, which are separated by agarose gel electrophoresis. Which of the following are correct?

(a) The 0.5 kb fragment moves farthest from the well.
(b) The 5 kb fragment stays closest to the well.
(c) After staining with ethidium bromide and exposure to UV radiation, three bright orange bands are seen.
(d) The fragments move towards the cathode (negative electrode).
(e) The 2 kb band can be cut out of the gel and the DNA extracted (eluted) for use in constructing recombinant DNA.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: DNA fragments are negatively charged and move towards the anode under an electric field; they separate according to size through the sieving effect of the agarose gel, so the smaller the fragment the farther it moves. Bands are seen after ethidium bromide staining and UV exposure as bright orange bands; the separated bands are cut out and extracted (elution), and the purified fragments are used in constructing recombinant DNA.
solution.why_others_wrong: DNA is negatively charged and moves to the anode, so (d) is false and every option containing it is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Separation and isolation of DNA fragments)
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b), (c) and (e) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Assume a DNA molecule whose sequence is random, with A, T, G and C equally frequent. On average, how many recognition sites of a restriction enzyme that recognises one specific 6-bp palindromic sequence (such as EcoRI's 5'-GAATTC-3') are expected in 409,600 bp of this DNA? (Count along one strand; because the site is palindromic, the other strand gives the same sites.)

solution.explanation: The chance that any given 6 consecutive bases match one specific sequence is (1/4)⁶ = 1/4096. So a 6-bp site is expected about once every 4096 bp. Expected sites = 409,600 / 4096 = 100.
solution.shortcut: A specific n-bp site occurs about once every 4ⁿ bp.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1,600 uses a 4-bp site (4⁴ = 256); 25 uses 4⁷; 68,267 divides by 6 instead of by 4⁶.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Restriction enzymes)
solution.final_answer: Option A: 100

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following methods introduce recombinant DNA into host cells WITHOUT using a 'disarmed pathogen' that infects the cell?

(a) Micro-injection of recombinant DNA into the nucleus of an animal cell
(b) Biolistics (gene gun) with DNA-coated gold or tungsten micro-particles
(c) Treatment of bacterial cells with calcium ions followed by a heat shock
(d) Use of the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens
(e) Use of disarmed retroviruses

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Methods of introducing DNA into hosts
solution.explanation: NCERT: in micro-injection recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell; in biolistics, cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA (suitable for plants); bacteria are made competent with a divalent cation such as calcium and given a heat shock. The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium and disarmed retroviruses are 'disarmed pathogen' vectors which, when allowed to infect the cell, transfer the recombinant DNA into the host.
solution.why_others_wrong: Agrobacterium (Ti plasmid) and retroviruses are pathogens modified to be harmless, so they are exactly the 'disarmed pathogen' vectors excluded by the question.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Insertion of recombinant DNA into the host cell/organism)
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In PCR, the DNA polymerase does not have to be added afresh after each denaturation step.
Reason (R): The thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from Thermus aquaticus remains active during the high temperature used for denaturation of double-stranded DNA.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why a thermostable polymerase is used
solution.explanation: NCERT: the PCR enzyme is a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus), which remains active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double-stranded DNA. Because the enzyme is not destroyed when the reaction is heated to separate the strands, the same enzyme works through repeated cycles. R explains A.
steps: So it need not be replaced each cycle -> R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: An ordinary polymerase would be inactivated at the denaturation temperature; the thermostability stated in R is exactly why A holds, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Amplification of gene of interest using PCR)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In PCR, the part of the template that gets amplified is decided by the primers, because the DNA polymerase extends the primers bound to complementary regions of the template.
Statement II: PCR can amplify a gene only after the gene has been cloned in a plasmid and introduced into a living host cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in PCR, multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest are synthesised in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA) and the enzyme DNA polymerase, which extends the primers. The primers therefore mark the ends of the amplified region. PCR is done in vitro; its product can later be ligated with a vector for cloning, but no host cell is needed for the amplification.
steps: Statement I: true - amplification runs between the primer-binding regions
Statement II: false - PCR is an in vitro method
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the order of events: PCR products may be cloned afterwards, but PCR itself needs no living cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology (Amplification of gene of interest using PCR)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (observation after transformation) with List-II (interpretation).

List-I:
A. With a vector carrying ampR and tetR, the insert placed in tetR: a colony grows on ampicillin but not on tetracycline
B. With the same vector: a colony grows on both ampicillin and tetracycline
C. A bacterium spread on an ampicillin plate does not grow at all
D. With a vector whose insert site lies in the β-galactosidase gene: a colony gives no colour with the chromogenic substrate

List-II:
I. Insertional inactivation of the β-galactosidase gene by the insert
II. The cell did not take up the vector
III. Transformant carrying the vector without an insert
IV. Insertional inactivation of the tetracycline resistance gene by the insert

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against these antibiotics, so a cell that does not grow on ampicillin has not taken up the vector. If foreign DNA is inserted within the tetracycline resistance gene, recombinants lose tetracycline resistance but still grow on ampicillin; non-recombinant transformants grow on both. With β-galactosidase as marker, colonies whose plasmid has an insert give no colour, while those without an insert give blue colonies.
steps: Grows on amp, not tet -> IV
solution.why_others_wrong: Growth on both antibiotics means both genes are intact (no insert), while loss of tetracycline resistance marks the recombinant; a colourless colony marks an insert in the β-galactosidase gene, not a cell without the vector.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Cloning vectors)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A researcher uses a vector whose only selectable marker is the ampicillin resistance gene, but by mistake the E. coli strain used as the host is already resistant to ampicillin. What problem will arise when the treated cells are plated on an ampicillin-containing medium?

options.text: No cells will grow, because the two resistance genes cancel each other
Only the recombinants will grow, because the insert inactivates the host's resistance gene
Non-transformants will also grow, so transformants cannot be distinguished from them
The vector will not replicate, because the host already has an origin of replication

solution.concept: Why the host must lack the marker
solution.explanation: NCERT: selectable markers help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants; antibiotic resistance genes are useful markers for E. coli because normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against these antibiotics. Only the transformants then grow on the antibiotic. If the host is already resistant, every cell grows, so transformants cannot be told apart from non-transformants.
steps: Selection works only if non-transformants are killed by the antibiotic
Host already resistant -> all cells grow -> no selection
solution.why_others_wrong: Resistance genes do not cancel; the insert sits in the vector, not in the host chromosome; and the vector's ori works independently of the host's own replication.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 9 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology (Cloning vectors)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Non-transformants will also grow, so transformants cannot be distinguished from them

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: NCERT lists several ways in which genetic modification has been useful in crop plants. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.text: Crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, salt and heat
Increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants

solution.explanation: NCERT: genetic modification has (i) made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), (ii) reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops), (iii) helped to reduce post-harvest losses, (iv) increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants, and (v) enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g. golden rice.
steps: Listed: stress tolerance, reduced reliance on pesticides, fewer post-harvest losses, better mineral use, better nutrition
Increased reliance on pesticides is the opposite of (ii)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are NCERT's own examples of the benefits of GM plants; pest-resistant GM crops reduce, not increase, the use of chemical pesticides.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, Ch 10 'Biotechnology and its Applications', Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture
